the wages it earns each month
the rent it receives each year
a pension it receives each week
quiz.question: Which of these is part of a household's wealth rather than its income?
quiz.explanation: Wealth is a stock of assets owned at a point in time, such as land. Wages, rent received and pension payments are flows of income over a period.

options: a higher poverty line in the richer one
a larger population in the richer one
less capital and skills per worker in the poorer one
a lower Gini coefficient in the poorer country than the richer one
quiz.question: Which is most likely to explain a lasting gap in income per head between two countries?
quiz.explanation: Income per head follows output per worker, which depends on the capital, skills and technology each worker has. A poverty line or a Gini coefficient describes a distribution; it does not cause the gap.

options: richer households save a larger share of their income
poorer households save a larger share of their income
saving is required by law of richer households
interest rates are higher for poorer households
quiz.question: Why might greater income inequality raise total saving in an economy?
quiz.explanation: A rich household cannot spend all it earns and saves much of it; a poor one spends almost everything. Shifting income towards the rich therefore tends to raise total saving.

options: narrow the pay gap between skilled and less-skilled workers
lower the pay of workers who design the new systems
reduce the returns to owning the firms that use it
widen the pay gap between skilled and less-skilled workers
quiz.question: Automation that replaces routine clerical jobs is most likely to:
quiz.explanation: Technology raises demand for the skilled workers who build and run it and cuts demand for routine work, so pay at the upper end rises relative to the rest.

options: below sixty per cent of median income in that country
lower than the average wage paid in that country
too low to own any wealth such as land or savings
too low to meet basic needs such as food and shelter
quiz.question: Absolute poverty is best defined as an income that is:
quiz.explanation: Absolute poverty is judged against a fixed line of survival needs, whatever others earn. A line set as a share of the median is the relative measure; owning no wealth is a different thing again.

options: the cost of a basket of food
the international poverty line
median income in that society
the highest income in that society
quiz.question: A relative poverty line is usually set as a fraction of:
quiz.explanation: Relative poverty compares a household with the typical income of its own society, so the line is a share of the median. A food basket and the international line are fixed benchmarks for absolute poverty.

options: fall sharply
stay the same
rise sharply as well
fall to zero
quiz.question: If every income in a country rose by 20%, relative poverty would most likely:
quiz.explanation: The median rises by 20% as well, so the relative line rises with it and the same people stay below it. Absolute poverty, measured against a fixed line, would fall.

flashcards.back: An income too low to meet basic needs — food, safe water, shelter, clothing — measured against a fixed line.
An income far below the typical income of one's own society, measured against a line set as a fraction (often 50% or 60%) of median income.

steps: Marenda's median income is $6.00 a day, so the relative line is $3.60 and 30% of people are below it.
The richest two tenths gain: their incomes rise to $16.40 and $37.00.
The Gini coefficient rises from 0.39 to 0.49: inequality has increased.
The median is still $6.00, so the relative line has not moved.
The share below it is still 30%: relative poverty is unchanged.
chains.title: Why a richer top does not change relative poverty
chains.result: Relative poverty compares the bottom with the middle, and inequality measures the whole spread. They can move separately, which is why a question on one should never be answered with the other.

evaluation.title: Is growth enough to end poverty?
evaluation.content: Growth has done more than anything else to reduce absolute poverty, but it does not reduce relative poverty unless the bottom gains faster than the middle. **The pattern of growth matters more than its rate.** Labour-intensive growth that raises wages at the bottom cuts poverty far more than growth from a mine or an oil field, and the tax revenue growth brings reduces poverty only if it is spent on the poor.
